claims.text: The initial alloy is as-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr maintains high strength from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.
Partial substitution of Hf by V will reduce the density of HfMoTaTiZr.
Partial substitution of Hf by V will not significantly degrade strength at room temperature or around 1000 °C.
The proposed intervention replaces 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of the Hf atoms with V while keeping the other elemental fractions constant.
The V-substituted alloy will retain a high-entropy, single-phase solid solution.
The V-substituted alloy will preserve lattice distortion and phase stability.
Preserving the proposed microstructure will maintain solid-solution strengthening.
Preserving precipitation strengthening will help maintain mechanical properties after Hf-to-V substitution.
Replacing heavy Hf with lighter V lowers the alloy's overall atomic weight and consequently its density.
V has high-temperature performance comparable enough to Hf to permit density reduction without a major loss of strength.
Compatible atomic-size mismatch and bonding between the constituent elements would allow the V-substituted alloy to retain a single-phase microstructure.
Increasing Hf-to-V substitution could reduce the heavy element's density contribution by approximately 10–20%.
Yield strength at room temperature and 1000 °C will decrease by less than approximately 10–15% relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The hypothesis applies from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C under tensile or compressive loading, provided the high-entropy structure remains stable.
The optimal Hf replacement fraction is unknown and may depend on processing conditions.
A strength loss greater than 10–15% or deleterious phase formation is specified as a rejection outcome.

contradictions.description: The proposed mediator requires retention of a single-phase solid solution while also invoking preservation of precipitation strengthening. Conventional precipitation strengthening entails a distinguishable precipitate population and therefore is not straightforwardly consistent with a strictly single-phase description.

The hypothesis allows that only an unknown optimal partial-substitution fraction may succeed, but the rejection rule states that failure of any tested V-substituted alloy falsifies the hypothesis. Failure at one substitution level would not logically reject the possibility that another level satisfies the hypothesis.
